Looking at this cartoon setup with two people on a hill with wine watching a winking moon-faced moon, let me evaluate these captions:

**Strongest contenders:**

**(B) "I've never seen this guy before in my life, Babe, I swear!"** - This is excellent. It creates an implied narrative where one person thinks the other has a connection/romantic history with the moon. The absurdity of defensively denying a relationship with the moon, combined with the specific phrase "Babe, I swear," gives it character and an unexpected angle. It plays on relationship dynamics in a funny way.

**(H) "Don't be fooled. He has a dark side."** - Clever wordplay using the astronomical fact of the moon's dark side while treating it as a personality warning. Very New Yorker-style sophistication.

**(J) "Oh, I didn't know we were going on THIS kind of trip."** - Good double meaning (journey vs. drug trip), suggesting they're hallucinating.

**Why (B) is funniest:**
- It has personality and an implied backstory
- The humor is unexpected and absurdist (defending yourself from lunar flirtation)
- It captures relationship dynamics in a relatable way
- The specificity of "Babe, I swear" adds comedic weight
- It's exactly the kind of character-driven humor the New Yorker favors

ANSWER: (B)
